nodes.title: Arnav's Brain
nodes.body:
# Arnav's Brain

**In one sentence:** My second brain as a 3D map that an AI agent grows every morning.

## What it does
- Every note in my Obsidian vault is a glowing node; every link is a line. Topics form their own regions.
- A scheduled Claude agent reads my sources each morning, writes new notes in my words, links them, and republishes the map.
- Privacy by design: only notes marked public are exported, links to private notes are stripped, and the export refuses to publish if any private text slips through.
- A private version on my laptop is my daily hub: briefing, sorted email, deadlines, life areas, files and flashcards.

## How it's built
React + Vite + Tailwind, Three.js via react-force-graph with a bloom pass, an export script with a leak check, and a local API that runs Claude Code for the private dashboard.

## Related
- [[Software]]
- [[Cramr]]

meta.summary: My second brain as a 3D map that an AI agent grows every morning from my email, files and notes.

# Cramr

**In one sentence:** An academic command center for college students: deadlines, grades, study time and workload in one place.

## What it does
- **Busy Score**: a 0–100 workload gauge computed from remaining hours, urgency, difficulty and deadline clustering.
- **Natural-language add**: "Calc problem set due Friday, 3 hours, hard" becomes a structured assignment via Gemini.
- **Study tools**: turn notes, files or a YouTube transcript into summaries, study guides or flashcards.
- **Grades**: weighted components, a what-you-need-on-the-final calculator, GPA tracking.
- **Canvas LMS sync**, a Pomodoro study timer with Focus Mode, a semester heatmap, and an AI weekly debrief.
- Installable PWA.

## How it's built
React 19 + Vite + Tailwind on the frontend (Vercel); Node/Express + SQLite + JWT auth on the backend (Fly.io); Docker for local dev.

## Timeline
- Jul 14–15, 2026: deployed (Vercel + Fly.io), added a landing page, rebranded from StudentHub to Cramr
- Jul 25, 2026: fixed PDF parsing, expanded the onboarding tour

## Related

nodes.title: STRANDED Minecraft Mod
nodes.body:
# STRANDED Minecraft Mod

**In one sentence:** A survival-horror Minecraft mod, loosely inspired by *Cast Away*: you're the only survivor of a helicopter crash on a remote island — and on the third night, you realize you're not alone.

## Design pillars
- **Linear progression** — 11 quests that must be done in order, tracked in a craftable Quest Journal.
- **Survival first** — every item has a grounded reason to exist (the starting kit: flares, matches, a signal mirror, a mylar blanket…).
- **Horror reveal** — the monster (the Wraith) is never announced; you first see it standing at the treeline.
- **Emotional arc** — hope, despair, grit, triumph. Day is warm and hopeful; night is oppressive.

## How it plays
- **Act I — Wake up, stay alive:** search the crash, first night, an SOS the plane doesn't answer.
- **Act II — Dig in:** shelter, map the island's 5 regions, find a previous castaway's camp and journal.
- **Act III — It's not just the island:** fire wards off the Wraith (campfire 12 blocks, torch 6, flare blinds it); craft a Bone Fire; build a raft.
- **Act IV — End it:** lure the Wraith into the Bone Fire's light, then sail home.

## Systems
- Progression locks: journal gate, recipe locks, a raft sail that only unlocks after the Wraith is dead, minimum in-game days.
- Cast Away easter eggs: Wilson, the unopenable FedEx package, "Noname Atoll", a loading-screen quote that changes.
- Scope: 1 biome, 1 custom mob, ~10 items, 1 multi-block raft, 11 quests, a text-overlay cutscene system.

## Related
- [[Software]]

nodes.title: Transfer Entropy Analysis
nodes.body:
# Transfer Entropy Analysis

**In one sentence:** Which tech stocks move first? I measured directional information flow between six large-cap tech stocks with [[Transfer Entropy]].

## Data
- Six tickers: AAPL, MSFT, NVDA, AMD, GOOGL, TSLA — same sector, so information flow between them has a plausible reason. 6 tickers = 30 directed pairs.
- Daily adjusted closes from Yahoo Finance, Aug 16 2019 – Aug 14 2024 (1,257 trading days).
- Converted prices to [[Log Returns]] first: raw prices trend upward, which breaks the estimator.

## The direction problem
PyIF's `te_compute(X, Y)` doesn't document which argument is the source. I read `helper.py`: it builds a space of X[t+1], X[t], Y[t] and computes I(X[t+1]; Y[t] | X[t]) — so `te_compute(X, Y)` = TE(Y → X). X is the target, Y the source. Guessing wrong would have flipped every result.

## Results
| Source → Target | TE | Net flow (source leads) |
|---|---|---|
| AMD → MSFT | 0.094 | +0.047 |
| AMD → NVDA | 0.083 | +0.180 |
| NVDA → MSFT | 0.079 | +0.085 |
| AMD → AAPL | 0.052 | +0.182 |
| GOOGL → NVDA | 0.023 | +0.104 |

- **AMD leads.** I expected NVDA to lead AMD; the data says the opposite. Plausible reason: AMD reacts faster to chip-demand signals (inventory, memory pricing, fab capacity), which reach NVDA the next day.
- **GOOGL absorbs, doesn't transmit.** Almost every GOOGL-as-source value was negative.
- Negative TE values just mean no meaningful flow — the Kraskov estimator dips below zero in finite samples.

## Limitations
- No permutation test (200 shuffles × 30 pairs = 6,000 runs), so some small positive values may be noise.
- Parameters: k = 1, one-day lag, n = 1,256.

## Related
- [[Data Science]]
- [[Finance]]
- [[Correlation]]

meta.summary: Measured which big tech stocks "lead" others day to day, using transfer entropy on five years of daily returns.

nodes.title: Beta
nodes.body:
# Beta

**In one sentence:** Beta measures how much a stock moves compared to the overall market.

## Notes
- Learned how to calculate it on .

> [!info] Added by Claude
> **Formula**
> $$\beta = \frac{\text{Cov}(R_i, R_m)}{\text{Var}(R_m)}$$
> - $R_i$ = the stock's returns, $R_m$ = the market's returns (usually the S&P 500)
> - Same thing as the **slope** when you regress the stock's returns on the market's returns
>
> **How to read it**
> | Beta | Meaning |
> |---|---|
> | β = 1 | Moves with the market |
> | β > 1 | More volatile than the market (e.g. 1.5 → ~15% move when market moves 10%) |
> | 0 < β < 1 | Less volatile than the market |
> | β < 0 | Tends to move opposite to the market |
>
> **In Excel/Sheets:** `=SLOPE(stock_returns, market_returns)` or `=COVARIANCE.S(stock, market)/VAR.S(market)`
>
> Beta only captures [[Systematic Risk]] (market-wide risk), not risk specific to one company. It's the key input to the [[CAPM]].

## Related
- [[Finance]]
- [[CAPM]]
- [[Systematic Risk]]
- [[Correlation]] — similar formula, different meaning
- [[Market Risk Premium]]
- [[Portfolio Beta]]

## Sources
- [[Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model]] (Lecture 13)

nodes.title: CAPM
nodes.body:
# CAPM

**In one sentence:** The expected return on any asset is equal to the risk-free return plus a premium that reflects the risk (as measured by [[Beta]]) of the asset.

## Notes
$$E(r_j) = r_f + \beta_j\,[E(r_M) - r_f]$$

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $E(r_j)$ | expected return on asset $j$ |
| $r_f$ | |
| $\beta_j$ | [[Systematic Risk]] of asset $j$ |
| $E(r_M) - r_f$ | [[Market Risk Premium]] (MRP) |
| $\beta_j[E(r_M) - r_f]$ | asset $j$'s risk premium |

- Measures systematic risk, not total risk, because [[Unsystematic Risk]] gets diversified away.
- Plotted, it's the [[Security Market Line]].
- ⚠️ Avoid: if you're given the MRP, don't subtract $r_f$ again. $0.03 + 1.50(0.08)$, not $0.03 + 1.50(0.08 - 0.03)$.

## Related
- [[Finance]]
- [[Beta]]
- [[Portfolio Beta]]

## Sources
- [[Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model]] (Lecture 13)

nodes.title: Correlation
nodes.body:
# Correlation

**In one sentence:** How much two variables move together, relative to the product of how much each one moves.

## Notes
$$\rho_{ij} = \frac{\sigma_{ij}}{\sigma_i\sigma_j}$$
- measures how much two variables move together; correlation scales that by both standard deviations.
- [[Beta]] looks similar (covariance in the numerator) but is importantly different:
$$\beta_i = \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_M^2} \neq \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_i\sigma_M} = \rho_{iM}$$
- Beta divides by the market's variance only, so it's movement *relative to the market*.

## Related
- [[Finance]]
- [[Beta]]
- [[Unsystematic Risk]]

## Sources
- [[Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model]] (Lecture 13)

# Effective Annual Rate

**In one sentence:** The rate you actually earn or pay in a year once compounding is counted.

## Notes
- The answer is always a **percentage**: if the calculation gives 4.17, the answer is 417%, not 4.17.

> [!info] Added by Claude
> $$EAR = \left(1 + \frac{APR}{m}\right)^{m} - 1$$
> $m$ = compounding periods per year.

# Log Returns

**In one sentence:** The daily change in a price, measured as a difference of logs, so it hovers around zero instead of trending up.

## Notes
$$r_t = \ln P_t - \ln P_{t-1}$$
- Raw prices trend over time, which breaks methods that expect stable data (like [[Transfer Entropy]]). Returns fluctuate around zero.
- You lose one observation (1,257 prices → 1,256 returns).

nodes.title: Market Risk Premium
nodes.body:
# Market Risk Premium

**In one sentence:** Market Risk Premium is NOT the same thing as market expected return.

## Notes
- Easy to mix these up. ⚠️

> [!info] Added by Claude
> **Market Risk Premium (MRP) = Expected market return − Risk-free rate**
> $$MRP = E(R_m) - R_f$$
> - **Market expected return** $E(R_m)$ = the *total* return you expect from the market (e.g. 10%)
> - **Market risk premium** = only the *extra* return on top of the risk-free rate, as a reward for taking risk (e.g. 10% − 4% = 6%)
>
> **Why it matters:** In the [[CAPM]], you multiply [[Beta]] by the **premium**, not the total return:
> $$E(R_i) = R_f + \beta \times (E(R_m) - R_f)$$
> Common mistake: using $E(R_m)$ where the formula needs $E(R_m) - R_f$. That double-counts the risk-free rate.
>
> **Watch the wording in problems:** "the market's expected return is 10%" → subtract $R_f$ yourself. "The market risk premium is 6%" → plug it in directly.

## Related
- [[Finance]]
- [[Beta]]
- [[CAPM]]
- [[Security Market Line]] — the MRP is its slope

## Sources
- [[Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model]] (Lecture 13)

nodes.title: Portfolio Beta
nodes.body:
# Portfolio Beta

**In one sentence:** A portfolio's beta and expected return are just the weighted averages of its assets'.

## Notes
$$\beta_p = \omega_X\beta_X + \omega_Y\beta_Y \qquad E(r_p) = \omega_X E(r_X) + \omega_Y E(r_Y) \qquad \omega_X + \omega_Y = 1$$
- Alternative: find $E(r_p)$ first, then solve the [[CAPM]] for $\beta_p$. Same answer.
- Wording trick: "three times as much in A as in B" → $\omega_A = 3\omega_B$ → $\omega_B = \tfrac14$.
- Example: 2/3 in X ($\beta = 1.66$), 1/3 in Y ($\beta = 0.62$) → $\beta_p = 1.31$.

## Related
- [[Finance]]
- [[Beta]]
- [[CAPM]]

## Sources
- [[Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model]] (Lecture 13)

- The market IS average. Beta is units of risk.
- Above the line = undervalued (U), below = overvalued (O).
- Undervalued assets have higher returns.

nodes.id: Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model
nodes.title: Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model
nodes.body:
# Risk and the Capital Asset Pricing Model

Lecture 13 — Risk & the Capital Asset Pricing Model ([[CAPM]]). Related: [[Finance]], [[Beta]], [[Market Risk Premium]], [[Systematic Risk]], [[Unsystematic Risk]], [[Security Market Line]], [[Correlation]], [[Portfolio Beta]], , .

## Equations
$$S = \frac{E(r_P) - r_f}{\sigma_P}$$
$$\omega_X = \frac{\sigma_Y^2 - \sigma_{XY}}{\sigma_X^2 + \sigma_Y^2 - 2\sigma_{XY}}$$
$$\sigma_{XY} = \sigma_X \sigma_Y \rho_{XY}$$
$$\sigma_P^2 = \omega_X^2\sigma_X^2 + \omega_Y^2\sigma_Y^2 + 2\omega_X\omega_Y\sigma_X\sigma_Y\rho_{XY}$$
$$E(r_P) = \omega_X E(r_X) + \omega_Y E(r_Y)$$

## Two big ideas over two weeks
| Risk & Return (ch 9) | Market Efficiency (ch 11) |
|---|---|
| The SML & CAPM | Kicking a rock – a short story |
| Beta vs Correlation | Prices & Information |
| Risk-free rates | Rolling dice & Throwing darts |
| Market return & MRP | Implications |
| Investing & Gambling | Reasons to Believe |
| Flipping coins | Evidence |

## Last week: Portfolios (efficient diversification)
- We do not like risk, but we do not generally avoid it
- We take risks because of the potential benefits
- In financial markets riskier assets provide higher returns
- Diversification reduces an investor's exposure to risk
- Not all risk can be diversified away

## Diversifiable risk
- The risks unique to individual assets are what lead to imperfect correlations between asset returns. Let's consider stocks.
- This "unique" risk can be diversified away by creating portfolios of individual stocks with imperfect correlations (varying "unique" risks).
- Heuristically:
$$\text{total risk} \equiv \text{systematic risk} + \text{unsystematic risk}$$

## Systematic risk
- Systematic risk is defined to be the risk inherent in all risky assets (stocks) and therefore cannot be diversified away by creating portfolios of stocks
- Some stocks have more systematic risk than other stocks
- Also commonly referred to as market risk, beta risk, and undiversifiable risk
- Examples: political risk, business cycles/economy, crude oil

## Unsystematic risk
- Unsystematic risk is unique to an individual stock (or a small group of stocks or even an industry) and therefore it can be diversified away by creating a portfolio of stocks.
- Some stocks have more unsystematic risk than other stocks.
- Also commonly referred to as unique risk, firm-specific risk, idiosyncratic risk, and diversifiable risk.
- Examples: legal issues, leadership, innovation

## This week: Individual risky assets
- Need a measure of risk that recognizes the elimination of unsystematic risk through diversification
- Measure systematic risk, not total risk
- Capital Asset Pricing Model and Beta as a measure of systematic risk.
- Next week we will link the portfolio theory from last week with the CAPM from this week as we explore further the role of information and the behavior of individual investors

## Capital Asset Pricing Model
$$E(r_j) = r_f + \beta_j\,[E(r_M) - r_f]$$

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $E(r_j)$ | expected return on asset $j$ |
| $r_f$ | risk-free rate of return |
| $\beta_j$ | systematic risk of asset $j$ |
| $E(r_M)$ | expected return on the market |
| $E(r_M) - r_f$ | market risk premium (MRP) |
| $\beta_j[E(r_M) - r_f]$ | asset $j$'s risk premium |

The expected return on any asset is equal to the risk-free return plus a premium that reflects the risk (as measured by beta) of the asset.

## The SML (CAPM)
- Slope is MRP: $E(r_M) - r_f$
- Market IS average
- Beta is units of risk
- Beta measures movement relative to market:
$$\beta_i = \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_M^2} \neq \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_i\sigma_M} = \rho_{iM}$$
- U is undervalued, O is overvalued (points above/below the SML on the slide graph).
- Undervalued assets have higher returns (time value of money)

## Correlation
$$\rho_{ij} = \frac{\sigma_{ij}}{\sigma_i\sigma_j} = \frac{\text{covariance of } i \text{ and } j}{(\text{std. dev. of } i)(\text{std. dev. of } j)}$$
- Covariance measures how much two variables move together
- Correlation measures how much two variables move together relative to the product of how much those two variables move
- Beta is similar to correlation (they both have covariance in the numerator), but importantly different from correlation.

## Beta
- Beta measures systematic risk (market risk, undiversifiable risk)
$$\beta_i = \frac{\sigma_{iM}}{\sigma_M^2} = \frac{\text{covariance of asset return with market return}}{\text{variance of market return}}$$
- Beta measures how much an asset's return moves together with the market return, relative to how much the market return moves

## Market Efficiency
- "Kicking a rock" (slides were title/image only — no text to capture)

---

## Examples

### Example A
Risk-free rate 3.0%, MRP 8.0%, $\beta_A = 1.50$, $\beta_B = 0.90$. Find $E(r_A)$ & $E(r_B)$.
- $E(r_A) = 0.03 + 1.50(0.08) = 0.1500$ → **15.0%**
- $E(r_B) = 0.03 + 0.9(0.08) = 0.1020$ → **10.20%**
- ⚠️ Avoid!!! $E(r_A) = 0.03 + 1.50(0.08 - 0.03) = 0.1050$ — MRP is already $E(r_M) - r_f$, don't subtract $r_f$ again (see [[Market Risk Premium]]).

Risk premiums for the two stocks:
- A: $1.50(0.08) = 0.1200$ → **12.0%**
- B: $0.1020 - 0.03 = 0.0720$ → **7.20%**

### Example B
Risk-free rate 1.5%, expected market return 9.0%, $E(r_X) = 13.95\%$, $E(r_Y) = 6.15\%$, $\beta_Z = 1.38$.
- $0.1395 = 0.015 + \beta_X(0.09 - 0.015)$ → $\beta_X = 1.66$
- $0.0615 = 0.015 + \beta_Y(0.09 - 0.015)$ → $\beta_Y = 0.62$
- $E(r_Z) = 0.015 + 1.38(0.09 - 0.015)$ → $E(r_Z) = 11.85\%$

Portfolio 2/3 in X, 1/3 in Y — use $E(r_p) = \omega_X E(r_X) + \omega_Y E(r_Y)$, $\beta_p = \omega_X\beta_X + \omega_Y\beta_Y$, $\omega_X + \omega_Y = 1$:
- $E(r_p) = \tfrac{2}{3}(0.1395) + \tfrac{1}{3}(0.0615) = 0.1135$ → **11.35%**
- $\beta_p = \tfrac{2}{3}(1.66) + \tfrac{1}{3}(0.62) = 1.3133$ → **1.31**
- Alternative: $0.1135 = 0.015 + \beta_p(0.09 - 0.015)$ → $\beta_p = 1.31$

### Example C
Risk-free rate 3.0%, MRP 8.0%, $\beta_A = 1.28$, $\beta_B = 0.80$.

$E(r_p)$ for 50/50 portfolio:
- $\beta_p = 0.50(1.28) + 0.50(0.80) = 1.04$
- $E(r_p) = 0.03 + 1.04(0.08) = 0.1132$ → **11.32%**
- Alternative?

$\beta_p$ if three times as much is invested in A than in B:
- $\omega_A = 3\omega_B$ → $3\omega_B + \omega_B = 1$ → $\omega_B = \tfrac{1}{4}$
- $\beta_p = 0.75(1.28) + 0.25(0.80) =$ **1.16**

### Example D
$r_f = 3.50\%$, $E(r_M) = 12.00\%$, $E(r_A) = 16.42\%$, $E(r_B) = 9.96\%$.

Weights for $E(r_p) = 12.50\%$:
- $0.1250 = 0.1642\,\omega_A + 0.0996(1 - \omega_A)$ → $\omega_A = 0.393188$
- **$\omega_A = 39.32\%$, $\omega_B = 60.68\%$**

Weights for $\beta_p = 0.90$:
- $E(r_p) = 0.035 + 0.90(0.120 - 0.035) = 0.1115$
- $0.1115 = 0.1642\,w + 0.0996(1 - w)$ → $w = 0.1842105$
- **A: 18.42%, B: 81.58%**

Portfolio with one-fourth as much invested in stock B as in stock A:
- $\omega_B = \tfrac{1}{4}\omega_A$ → $\omega_A + \tfrac{1}{4}\omega_A = 1$ → $\omega_A = 0.80$
- $E(r_p) = 0.80(0.1642) + 0.20(0.0996) = 0.15128$ → **15.13%**
- $0.1513 = 0.035 + \beta_p(0.085)$ → $\beta_p = 1.368235$ → **1.37**

## Source
- Lecture slides: `30026flecture13.pdf` (Lecture 13, 23 slides)

nodes.body:
# The Epidemic of Sports Betting

My presentation. **Thesis:** legalization of sports betting → rapid growth → money and risk impacts.

## Growth
- Betting on wins, scores and props; apps make it easy. About half of adults bet (Pew 2023).
- **2018: Murphy v. NCAA** — the Supreme Court let states decide. Phone betting spread fast.
- 35+ states now allow it; ads and social media normalize it, and college students are constantly exposed.

## Impacts
- **Money:** billions in bets and taxes, some funding programs like education (AGA 2024).
- **Engagement:** games feel more interactive; friends compete and discuss (Pew 2023).
- **Addiction:** apps make it accessible to young adults — risky habits and potential addiction (NCPG 2024).

**Takeaway:** enjoy responsibly — balance fun with caution.

## Related
- [[Finance]]

nodes.title: Transfer Entropy
nodes.body:
# Transfer Entropy

**In one sentence:** Does knowing A's past help predict B's next value, beyond what B's own past already tells you? If yes, information flows from A to B.

## Notes
$$TE(A \to B) = I(B_{t+1};\, A_t \mid B_t)$$
- It's **directional**: TE(A → B) and TE(B → A) can be completely different. That asymmetry is the point — unlike [[Correlation]], which is symmetric.
- Works on stationary data, so use [[Log Returns]], not prices.
- Small negative estimates (Kraskov kNN estimator) mean "no flow", not negative information.
- Check significance with a permutation test: shuffle the source, rebuild the null distribution.

## Related

nodes.title: Unsystematic Risk
nodes.body:
# Unsystematic Risk

**In one sentence:** Risk unique to one stock (or a small group of stocks, or an industry), so it can be diversified away.

## Notes
- Also called unique risk, firm-specific risk, idiosyncratic risk, or diversifiable risk.
- It's what makes asset returns imperfectly correlated, which is exactly why diversification works.
- Examples: legal issues, leadership, innovation.
- total risk ≡ [[Systematic Risk]] + unsystematic risk

## Related
